method: Round three of 1776, under the rule 'every story alike' (11 November 2026): the reports of Cherokee and Creek plans that rounds one and two held back for framing, counted item by item at the year's rule of 7 newspapers with phrase searches on all 2,319 pages in both transcriptions, reading of every hit, loose keyword searches of the papers in print without a hit, and scan checks of each admitted passage
scan_scope: Each crop covers the excerpt, the opening of the printed item. Long documents were not proofread in full.

new_groups.label: Henry Stuart's letter to the frontier inhabitants, May 1776
new_groups.definition: Printings of a letter to the settlers on the Watauga and Nolachucky rivers, signed 'Henry Stuart, Deputy Superintendent', for the British superintendent of Indian affairs in the southern district, with a sworn statement that a stranger delivered it on 18 May 1776. The letter invites those 'willing to join his Majesty's forces, as soon as they arrive at the Cherokee nation' to sign a paper of allegiance, and says that the King will land an army in West Florida and march it through the Creek nation to the Chickasaws, 'where 500 warriors from each nation are to join them', and on by the Cherokees, 'who have also promised their assistance'. The papers printed it in June and July as a letter delivered to the frontier inhabitants, and from late August among papers sent from Augusta, Georgia, as 'an intercepted letter'. One side's letter, as printed.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan (round three: stories once held back for framing, at the year's 7-paper rule).

new_groups.label: A letter from Savannah River, 13 May 1776: the Creek chiefs and the Cherokee towns
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Savannah River dated 13 May 1776, printed from Charleston (31 May): the writer reports that the Creek chiefs who were expected 'are down, and seem well disposed', and that letters from the Cherokees say the middle and lower towns will have no hand in it 'if the Over-hills are for mischief with the white people'; Henry Stewart and Captains Colbert and Gist (printed with the long s, 'Giſt', which the transcriptions read as 'Gift') are in the Over-hills with ammunition brought up the Mississippi, and were attacked on the way by 'the northward Indians'. One writer's report.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1776 printings, checked against the scan (round three: stories once held back for framing, at the year's 7-paper rule).

dispositions_summary.method: Round three of 1776. On 11 November 2026 the owner set the rule 'every story alike': a reviewed story is described by what kind of text it is and whose account, in the papers' own words, never as what happened; sensitive subjects get no special treatment. Items that earlier rounds held back for framing are therefore counted by the year's own rule, exactly like any other item: what reaches it is admitted, what does not stays out. As before, an excerpt ends before the names of private people where it can, and stories that turn on private people stay out. Rounds one and two left out the reports of Cherokee and Creek plans, each counted by the item finder in 8 papers. Both were read again with phrase searches over all 2,319 pages of 1776 in both transcriptions (phrase_patterns_round3.json, phrase_hits_round3.json), every hit was read, the papers in print in their weeks without a hit were searched with loose keywords (no missed printing), and every printing was checked against its page scan by AI reviewers (scan_batches/batch_16.json and batch_17.json, SCAN_PROTOCOL.md, scan_points_round3.json).
dispositions_summary.selection_rule: As in rounds one and two: a story needs one printed item found in 7 or more newspapers, counted item by item. Round one listed both items among its candidates in 7 or 8 papers; round two admitted every other listed candidate that reached 7. Both reach 8, so both are admitted, as two single stories.

counted_item_by_item.Henry Stuart's letter: Printed in two settings: from Virginia in June and July under the heading 'Copy of a letter addressed to the frontier inhabitants…' (VGB 7 June, NYP 20 June, PL 29 June, PP and NYG 1 July, FJ 13 July: 6 papers), and from 31 August among papers sent from Augusta, Georgia, to the Governor of Georgia, as 'an intercepted letter', after two sworn depositions (PEP 31 August, PG 4 September, PL 7 September, NYG 9 September). The letter is the same item in both, so they count together: 8 papers, 10 printings. The NYP continued its printing of 20 June in the issue of 27 June (page 3), counted once.
counted_item_by_item.The Savannah River letter: One item in 8 papers (NYP 4 July to FJ 27 July), printed from Charleston (31 May) in four of them.

not_admitted.Other reports of the southern frontier i: Letters from Fincastle of late July, an express on the relief of the Watauga fort, and a September paragraph of letters from the south on the war against the lower towns each reach 7 papers by the item finder. Round one read them among the 101 documents in 7 or more papers and did not choose them, like other 7- and 8-paper items; it did not record them as held back for framing. They can be read in a later round with the other items round one did not choose.
not_admitted.Still out by earlier decisions: The committees' notices under the bills resolution (they publish the names of private people; the owner's decision of 9 November 2026) and the parody of the Howes' September declaration (4 papers).
